title: OSI & TCP/IP Layers: Quick Revision Notes
summary: Night-before revision of the OSI seven layers and the TCP/IP four-layer model: what each layer does, PDUs, encapsulation, protocols and devices per layer, and hubs vs switches vs routers.

chapters.title: Layered Model Mental Map
points: Layering splits networking into stacked jobs: each layer serves the one above and talks to the same layer on the peer host
OSI 7 layers top to bottom: Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical (mnemonic: All People Seem To Need Data Processing)
TCP/IP 4 layers: Application, Transport, Internet, Link (Network Access)
OSI to TCP/IP mapping: L5-L7 collapse into Application; L4 = Transport; L3 = Internet; L1-L2 = Link
OSI is a reference model for reasoning and troubleshooting; TCP/IP is what is actually implemented

chapters.title: What Each OSI Layer Does
points: L7 Application: network services for apps and user-facing protocols (HTTP, DNS, SMTP)
L6 Presentation: encoding, encryption and compression (TLS, JPEG, ASCII/UTF-8 translation)
L5 Session: opens, maintains and closes dialogues between hosts (checkpointing, RPC sessions)
L4 Transport: end-to-end delivery between processes using ports; reliability, ordering, flow control (TCP) or none (UDP)
L3 Network: logical IP addressing and routing between networks; L2 Data Link: MAC addressing, framing, error detection (FCS) within one link; L1 Physical: bits as signals over cable, fibre or radio

chapters.title: PDUs and Encapsulation
points: PDU names: L7-L5 data/message, L4 segment (TCP) or datagram (UDP), L3 packet, L2 frame, L1 bits
Sending host encapsulates downward: data + TCP header = segment; + IP header = packet; + Ethernet header and FCS trailer = frame
Only the Data Link layer adds a trailer (FCS); the other layers add headers only
Receiving host de-encapsulates upward, each layer strips and reads its own header, then hands the payload up
Header fields to know: L4 = source/destination port; L3 = source/destination IP and TTL; L2 = source/destination MAC and EtherType

chapters.title: Protocols and Addresses by Layer
points: L7: HTTP/HTTPS, DNS, SMTP, FTP, SSH, DHCP; L6: TLS/SSL (often placed at L5-L6); L4: TCP (reliable, 3-way handshake SYN/SYN-ACK/ACK) and UDP (connectionless, low overhead)
L3: IP, ICMP (ping, traceroute), IPsec; routing protocols OSPF and BGP; L2: Ethernet, ARP (maps IP to MAC, often called L2.5), VLAN 802.1Q, PPP
Addressing per layer: port (L4) identifies the process, IP (L3) identifies the host and network, MAC (L2) identifies the NIC on the local link
MAC and IP change differently: the MAC address is rewritten at every hop, the IP address stays end to end (unless NAT)
Use TCP for web, email and file transfer; UDP for DNS lookups, VoIP, streaming and games

chapters.title: Devices, Hubs vs Switches vs Routers, Troubleshooting
points: Hub (L1): repeats every bit out all other ports, one shared collision domain and one broadcast domain, half duplex
Switch (L2): learns source MACs into a CAM table and forwards frames only to the destination port; each port is its own collision domain, all ports share one broadcast domain (unless VLANs)
Router (L3): forwards packets by destination IP using a routing table; each interface is its own broadcast domain, and it connects different networks
Layer 3 switch routes between VLANs at hardware speed; firewalls work at L3/L4 (stateful) up to L7 (application-aware); load balancers are L4 or L7

Bottom-up troubleshooting: check cable/link light (L1), then ARP/MAC and VLAN (L2), then ping and routes (L3), then port and firewall (L4), then app logs (L7); common mistakes: calling a router's job a switch's, saying ping tests TCP (it is ICMP at L3), placing TLS only at L7

chapters.title: OSI and TCP/IP Cheat Sheet
points: Layers with PDU: L7/6/5 data, L4 segment, L3 packet, L2 frame, L1 bits
Layer to address: L4 port, L3 IP, L2 MAC
Layer to device: L1 hub/repeater, L2 switch/bridge, L3 router, L4-L7 firewall and load balancer
Layer to protocol: L7 HTTP DNS SMTP SSH, L4 TCP UDP, L3 IP ICMP, L2 Ethernet ARP
Domains: hub = 1 collision + 1 broadcast; switch = per-port collision, 1 broadcast; router = per-interface broadcast
